opus-5.5.text:
I think the prospects are quite good, and it's one of the more promising areas for AI to help society handle the transition well.

Forecasting has some properties that make it a natural fit. You get feedback: events resolve, and you can score whether a system's probability for a recession, an election, or a policy's effects was well calibrated. That gives you a training signal and a way to build trust that doesn't depend on taking anyone's word for it. Human forecasting tournaments have already shown that careful, aggregated, calibrated judgment beats pundits and many experts. AI systems can do that kind of work at enormous scale: reading every relevant document, running many scenarios, updating continuously, and doing it for thousands of questions no human team could afford to cover.

On funding, there's a commercial engine. Hedge funds, insurers, and corporate strategy departments already pay a lot for better predictions, so a lot of capability will get built regardless. The gap is in public-interest questions: forecasting the consequences of government policies, or questions about AI development itself, where there's no market to capture the value. That's where philanthropy and governments can add a lot, by funding benchmarks, building question datasets with good resolution criteria, and supporting forecasts that are open and auditable rather than proprietary.

There are real challenges. Policy consequences are harder to score than near-term events, because the counterfactual isn't observed and the payoff horizons are long. You have to worry about systems being optimized to sound authoritative rather than to be right, and about who controls the system and whether its outputs get shaded toward someone's interests. So I'd want a lot of emphasis on track records, transparency, and multiple independent systems that can check each other.

The reason I care about this is that, as AI accelerates things, decision-makers will face very rapid change with less time to deliberate. Having trustworthy, calibrated advisors that can say "if you pass this policy, here's the likely distribution of outcomes," and that have earned trust through a verifiable record, could matter a great deal for avoiding catastrophic mistakes. It's an area where differential investment in beneficial capabilities seems clearly worthwhile.

r001.rationale: The response discusses forecasting policy effects, but does not say that forecasts of voters’ future reactions could shift political discourse.

r002.rationale: It says commercially valuable predictions will attract investment, while public-interest policy forecasts lack a market to capture their value, creating a financing gap.

r003.rationale: It mentions government funding generally, but not government misinformation programmes as a funding source.

r004.rationale: It calls for transparency and independent checks, but does not suggest requiring observable bias tests as a condition for government deployment.

fable-5.1.text:
Carl Shulman: I think this is one of the more underrated opportunities out there, and I'd put it in the category of things that look clearly good on multiple worldviews but that no existing actor is particularly incentivized to build well.

Let me lay out the basic case. We already have decent evidence from the forecasting literature — Tetlock's work on superforecasters, the various prediction tournaments, the metaculus-style aggregation platforms — that systematic forecasting with feedback and calibration beats the kind of pundit commentary and internal government estimates that actually drive most decisions. And the striking thing is how cheap that improvement was. We're talking about modest numbers of motivated amateurs, some training in base rates and probability decomposition, and a scoring rule. That's it. So there's low-hanging fruit that's been sitting there for over a decade.

Now add in what's happened with language models. You have systems that can read essentially every relevant document, every academic paper on, say, the effects of minimum wage changes or the historical track record of sanctions regimes, and that can do this at a scale no human analyst can. The early results on getting these systems to forecast are mixed — they're not yet at superforecaster level on most questions — but the trajectory is quite clear, and the cost per forecast is going to fall by orders of magnitude. So I expect that within a few years you'll be able to get something like superforecaster-quality probability estimates on enormous numbers of questions, including questions nobody bothered to ask because it wasn't worth a human's time.

Why does this matter? The standard thing I'd point to is that governments make trillions of dollars of decisions a year with remarkably little calibrated feedback. A central bank or a legislature making a policy choice is relying on models that are often never checked against outcomes, or on advisors whose track records are never scored. If you could attach honest, calibrated forecasts to proposed policies — here's what this bill does to employment, here's the probability this intervention escalates — you change the epistemic environment in which decisions are made. And I think the gains are large even if only a fraction of decision-makers pay attention, because the ones who do will tend to do better and that tends to be noticed.

The second thing, which I care about a lot more, is the AI governance angle specifically. We're heading into a period where the most important decisions about AI development and deployment are going to be made under enormous uncertainty, with strong commercial and geopolitical pressures, and where the costs of getting it wrong are potentially catastrophic. Having trusted, auditable forecasting systems that can say "if you adopt this policy, here's the distribution of outcomes" is one of the few mechanisms I can see for actually improving those decisions rather than just hoping the right people happen to be in the room. And it's a domain where you want the capability developed in a way that's transparent and that has a track record, so that when it matters people actually believe it.

So on the funding side, why hasn't this already happened? The incentives are poor. Private firms will build forecasting systems for financial markets, where you can monetize the edge, but political and policy forecasting has public-good characteristics — the value accrues diffusely to everyone who benefits from better governance, and there's not an obvious customer. Governments are institutionally resistant because scored forecasting creates accountability that officials don't want. And academic incentives reward novel methods papers, not the unglamorous work of running a forecasting system for years and tracking calibration. So you've got a classic market failure, and that's exactly the kind of gap philanthropy is well-placed to fill.

In terms of what I'd actually want funded: first, the infrastructure for evaluating these systems — large question banks with resolved outcomes, so you can actually tell whether a model is calibrated rather than just confident-sounding. Second, the research on getting AI systems to forecast well and, crucially, to explain their reasoning in ways humans can check, because a black-box number isn't going to move policy. Third, the institutional work of getting these forecasts in front of decision-makers in formats they can use, which is honestly as hard as the technical part. And fourth, work on the failure modes — these systems can be gamed, they can be manipulated by whoever controls the training data or the question selection, and they can give false confidence. You want people thinking about that before these things are influential rather than after.

My honest assessment is that the expected value per dollar here is high relative to a lot of what gets funded, the downside risks are manageable if you're attentive to them, and the main constraint is finding competent people and organizations to execute. It's not a case where throwing a billion dollars at it tomorrow would obviously work — you'd be funding a field into existence, and that's slow. But tens of millions over several years, well-targeted, could plausibly build something that persists and compounds. I'd be quite enthusiastic about more funders moving into this space.

r001.rationale: The response says forecasts could improve policy decisions, but does not suggest forecasting voters’ reactions to policies or shifting political discourse.

r002.rationale: It describes large potential benefits for governance while noting weak private incentives, diffuse public-good value, and no obvious customer for policy forecasting.

r003.rationale: It does not identify government misinformation programmes as a possible funding source.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest requiring observable bias tests as a condition for deploying AI in government.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a pretty promising area to fund, particularly because there’s a public goods problem. If you can forecast asset prices, there’s a fairly direct way to make money from that. If you can forecast the effects of a government policy, the benefits may be spread across millions of people, and there isn’t necessarily someone with an incentive to pay for the forecast and make it public.

One thing I’d be excited about is building a track record on questions where we can actually check the answers. You want to know whether these systems are well calibrated, whether they outperform existing forecasting methods, and whether they add information beyond what’s already reflected in markets or expert opinion. And you want that evaluation to be prospective: make the predictions, record them, and then see what happens.

Forecasting the consequences of policies is harder than forecasting events, because you don’t get to observe what would have happened under the policy you didn’t choose. A system could be good at predicting which countries will grow quickly without being good at telling you which intervention would increase growth. So you need to distinguish those capabilities.

But there’s potentially a lot of value here. Relatively modest philanthropic funding could support independent evaluations, public forecasts, and experiments with how policymakers use them. The key is to establish that you’re getting reliable additional information, and then find ways for that information to affect decisions.

r001.rationale: The response discusses forecasting policy effects and how policymakers might use forecasts, but does not mention predicting voters’ reactions or shifting political discourse.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the broad, dispersed public benefit of forecasting government policy effects with the lack of an obvious payer, while saying modest philanthropic funding could support the work.

r003.rationale: No government misinformation programmes or related funding source is identified.

r004.rationale: The response calls for evaluations of forecasting accuracy and added information, but does not propose bias tests as a condition for government AI deployment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a pretty strong case for funding that work, particularly as a way to improve decision-making about AI itself. Governments are going to face consequential choices about how quickly to deploy these systems, what safeguards to require, and how to respond to developments abroad. Better forecasts could help them distinguish policies that sound good from policies that actually produce good outcomes.

One difficulty is that forecasting what will happen is easier to evaluate than forecasting what would happen under a policy you don’t adopt. If a system assigns probabilities to election outcomes or economic growth, you can eventually score those predictions. If it says a particular regulation would increase growth, you don’t get to observe both the world with that regulation and the world without it. So I’d want funding to support rigorous evaluation, including being explicit about uncertainty, rather than just producing persuasive policy analysis.

There’s also a public-good aspect. A company can profit from forecasts that help it trade, but it may capture very little of the benefit from helping a government avoid a major policy mistake. That creates a potential role for philanthropy and public funding. I’d be interested in starting with relatively concrete, testable applications and expanding as there’s evidence that the systems improve on the alternatives.

r001.rationale: The response discusses forecasts helping governments assess policy outcomes, but does not mention forecasting voters’ reactions or shifting political discourse.

r002.rationale: It says avoiding major government policy mistakes could have public value that companies may not capture, creating a role for philanthropy and public funding.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify government misinformation programmes as a potential funding source.

r004.rationale: The response does not suggest requiring AI systems to pass observable bias tests before government deployment.
